brief.head: Partial outsider
brief.text: Amit Varma borrowed Janan Ganesh’s phrase for someone connected to a field but not bound by its conventions. He called it one of his great advantages. {113-C02}

brief.head: Google’s broken deal
brief.text: Media sites once let Google crawl their content in return for traffic, Ajay Shah said. Now an AI answer sits on top, and click-throughs have collapsed. {113-C05}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on how the news lost its way
lead.head: Eight crises, no villains
body: Ajay Shah grew up among journalists. From the age of six, he lived in a housing complex where 80 households all worked in the Indian media, and to him the trade was “fully a noble calling”. {113-S01}

Amit Varma, who came to journalism by accident around 2001, saw a more complicated world. Here he set out what went wrong, as eight crises: of relevance, purpose, money, quality, trust, power, incentives and attention.

He insisted the story had no villains, only structures and incentives. He had prepared by talking again to three journalists who had been guests on his podcast, *The Seen and the Unseen*: Prem Panicker, Shephali Bhatt and Samarth Bansal.
## Too much information
Journalism began, Varma argued, because information was scarce. A town crier offered a tiny nugget in the evening, and people valued whoever brought it. That is no longer true. {113-C01}

“Today information is abundant,” he said. “There is practically too much information.” The old institutions linger like artefacts, and people swiping on Instagram are not to blame: their needs are met elsewhere.

Shah objected that truth is still scarce, because corporations, governments and parties organise themselves to lie. Varma agreed that a good newspaper should filter for the truth, but said the mainstream media had abdicated that role.
## Follow the money

Purpose collided with profit. A newspaper is a business with shareholders, Varma said, and newsrooms came to be treated as cost centres. One editor told a journalist he spoke to that the job was to comfort the comforted.
Then the internet made advertising the only way to earn online, with the page view as its unit. As sites multiplied, page views lost value, the way money does when its supply grows. {113-C04}

A race to the bottom followed: clickbait, SEO headlines, articles chopped into pages. Senior people were sacked, specialist beats were cut, and reporters became generalists filing three stories a day.
Shah offered the cleanest evidence. Bennett Coleman, long the one Indian media house that reliably made money, went all in on tabloids and clickbait. Its operating profit fell significantly.

Quality was never as high as nostalgia suggests, Varma said, and now readers can compare. Specialists write online for themselves, and readers who spot a paper’s errors in their own field stop trusting the rest.
The state, meanwhile, wields a stick and a carrot: raids on owners’ other businesses, sacked editors, police visits, and government advertising that can be withdrawn. {113-C13}

And attention has fragmented, with algorithms feeding each reader more of what they clicked. “Two young people meeting each other is also in a sense two algorithms meeting each other,” Varma said. {113-C18}
## No easy answers

Varma had promised Shah some hope in the last chapter. There was little. Solo creators on Substack and YouTube now do some of the sense-making, he said, but he could not say who would cover the municipality and the flyover.

Shah’s answer was firms with business models. The convincing successes so far, he said, are old media that remade themselves: the Financial Times, the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and The Economist.
He also relayed a hopeful theory from his friend Suyash Rai. Radio was a weapon for Hitler and Mussolini before societies absorbed it, and today almost nobody takes WhatsApp forwards seriously.
“The people are not indefinitely stupid,” Shah said. “The people are stupid for some time.”

second.label: The page-view era
second.head: A lakh beats a crore
second.deck: At Yahoo India, a Bollywood party photographer outdrew award-winning long-form reporting
body: Around 2009 or 2010, Prem Panicker ran editorial at Yahoo India, where Amit Varma freelanced for him. The India team was set a target of 500 million page views a month. {113-S03}
Panicker’s Originals section produced deeply researched long-form reporting on a budget of more than a crore a year. Many pieces won awards, and each drew 40,000 or 50,000 page views. {#forty}

Then there was OMG, fed by one Bombay photographer paid a lakh a month to shoot Bollywood parties. It drew 450 to 500 million page views on its own. The higher-ups told Panicker his return on investment did not compare, and Originals was shut down.

quote.text: With that kind of investment we are getting these kind of page views. Your ROI doesn’t compare.

second.caption: the party photographer who outdrew Originals

third.head: Show us the paper
body: When Siddhartha Mukherjee, author of *The Emperor of All Maladies*, wrote in the New Yorker about India’s excess Covid deaths, he interviewed Ajay Shah over video. Shah had one of the first papers on the subject. {113-S08}
The magazine’s checkers confirmed every sentence attributed to him. That was not enough. “Show us the paper. Show us that you have backup for the claims that you made,” Shah recalled them saying.
All that for one paragraph of a 20,000-word story. Quality, T.N. Ninan once told Shah, needs enough man-hours at a high enough price per hour. Only Bennett Coleman could afford it, and it would not.
So India is stuck, Shah argued: chronically under-resourced journalism produces low quality, and the industry then concludes nobody will pay. {113-C10}
third.caption: the New Yorker’s fact-checkers

p2.title: Where it went wrong
p2.deck: Amit Varma’s diagnosis, crisis by crisis, with Ajay Shah adding evidence, objections and a little hope

sections.label: Crisis One
sections.head: The match you already saw
sections.caption: information that is no longer scarce
body: Journalism is older than the newspaper, Amit Varma argued. Town criers and the poets who carried oral histories met three needs: to know what was happening, to preserve it and to debate it.
Over time it added truth-seeking, sense-making and, in the 20th century, a watchdog role. Thucydides, Varma noted, is often called the first journalist for how rigorously he checked his sources.
But its founding reason was scarcity. “Today information is abundant. There is practically too much information. It is no longer a scarce resource,” he said. {113-C01}
## Ball by ball
Varma had seen this in miniature as a cricket writer in the early 2000s. Readers had already watched the match on television, so the ball-by-ball account had become a commodity. {113-S02}
British papers led the change. Cricket writers had to bring perspective and colour instead, and the writing grew richer.

Today sense-makers are everywhere, Varma said, and many are specialists who do the job better than generalist journalists. People swiping on Instagram are not at fault; their needs are being met elsewhere.

Ajay Shah pushed back. Information may be plentiful, he said, but truth is not: corporations, governments and political parties organise themselves to lie, and tribal nonsense such as anti-vax sentiment spreads.

~ Varma agreed that a good newspaper should filter its way to the truth. But his own most trusted filters are individuals: newsletters on Substack, the blog Marginal Revolution, people he follows on Twitter.

quote.text: A good newspaper should be a filter to the truth.

sections.label: Crisis Two
sections.head: Dharma versus the payroll
sections.caption: the editor who would comfort the comforted
body: Every profession has a kind of dharma, Amit Varma said, using the word loosely. Journalism’s higher purposes took shape only in the 20th century: seeking truth, speaking truth to power, afflicting the comfortable and comforting the afflicted.
Yet the editor of a major Indian newspaper told one of the journalists Varma spoke to that the job was to comfort the comforted. “And he meant it seriously,” Varma said. {113-S04}
Varma called the statement rational. A newspaper is a business, with shareholders and employees to answer to. An individual can put purpose before profit; a firm has fiduciary duties.
## A cost centre

Shephali Bhatt told him that her first newsroom, in her early twenties, treated journalists as a cost centre. Varma also recalled Vineet Jain telling the New Yorker that his company was in the advertising business, not the news business. {113-C03}
None of this was an accusation, Varma insisted. “There are no villains in this story,” he said. {#novillains}
~ Ajay Shah remembered the older bargain. In the complex where he grew up, journalists were poorly paid and there was little profit in the trade, “but there was a sense of purpose”.

quote.text: Vineet Jain famously said to the New Yorker, we are not in the news business, we are in the advertising business.

sections.label: Crisis Three
sections.head: Printing page views
sections.caption: page views inflated like a currency
body: In the early 2000s, Amit Varma said, advertising was the only way to make money online. People expected content to be free, as music had been in the days of Napster, and the unit sold was the page view.
As sites multiplied, so did page views, and each was worth less. “Now in the same way that in the economy, if you increase the money supply, inflation happens,” he said. {113-C04}

The race to the bottom brought clickbait, SEO headlines and pagination, which split an 800-word piece into four pages. As managing editor of Cricinfo, Varma refused. “It is in fact rude to make the reader click again,” he said. {113-S05}
## Where the money went
From 2010 to 2020, Samarth Bansal told him, outlets such as Vox, Vice and BuzzFeed were promised traffic for original content. The advertising went to Facebook, YouTube and Instagram instead.
For media, Varma said, advertising is dead. Writers can now earn from their audiences directly, through subscriptions, courses and communities. {113-C06}

~ Cost-cutting took the beats first: the municipality, the RBI, the dusty flyover. Nobody pays for them, but Bansal sees a civic purpose in them. “You are writing this first draft of history, which will often be the only draft of history,” Varma said. {113-C09}

quote.text: I don’t need the Times of India and I don’t need advertisers. I can go directly to my audience and monetise my audience.

sections.label: Crises Four and Five
sections.head: A mile wide, an inch deep
sections.caption: selection bias and Gell-Mann amnesia
body: The quality of Indian journalism was never what nostalgia suggests, Amit Varma argued. People remember Arun Shourie, Vir Sanghvi’s Sunday and India Today’s copy desk under Dilip Bobb, but those were outliers, and memory is biased towards them. {113-S07}
Before the internet, readers had nothing to compare with, so low standards bred low expectations.

Ajay Shah blamed resources. Journalists in India are singularly underpaid, he said, citing his friend Ashima Sharma, and quality takes costly process. The industry under-invests, produces low quality, and then concludes nobody will pay. {113-C10}
He hopes patient investors will fund five years of quality first. Varma is sceptical.
## Readers who know better

Trust fell with quality. Varma described Gell-Mann amnesia: a reader sees that a story on her own field is rubbish, then trusts the rest of the paper. “Why do you assume they reported everything else right?” he asked. {113-C11}
Now specialists such as Tyler Cowen on economics and Eric Topol on medicine write directly, and readers can see the gap.
~ Varma quoted Prem Panicker’s verdict: the Indian media is “a mile wide and an inch deep”. {113-J18}

quote.text: We are under investing in quality and that creates a chronic inability to monetise and then we are stuck.

sections.label: Crisis Six
sections.head: Asked to bend, they crawled
sections.caption: the state’s stick and carrot
body: Power here means the state, Amit Varma said. During the Emergency, Ramnath Goenka ran a blank page in the Indian Express, but most of the press capitulated. As L.K. Advani put it, “they were asked to bend, they chose to crawl”. {113-J15}

Owners once used their papers as a hedge against the state. The Singhanias started the Indian Post during their battle with the Wadias. Today, Varma said, corporate barons buy media houses to do the government a favour. “You can’t hedge against the state.” {113-C13}
## Stick and carrot

The stick is pressure on owners’ other businesses: a group that also owns chemical factories can be raided by the ED. The carrot is advertising from government, PSUs and parties, which can be withdrawn at any time.

Ajay Shah added conference income, which depends on ministers turning up, and op-ed space handed to serving officials. “Why will I pay a subscription for a newspaper?” he asked. “If you’re going to give me Doordarshan.” {113-C14}

~ Some incentives are written into rules. Varma relayed Ashok Malik’s argument that television news shouts because the government capped what channels could charge subscribers, leaving them dependent on advertising. {113-C15}

quote.text: A minister in a government has the editor of one of the biggest newspapers in the country summarily sacked, and he left the country.

sections.label: The future
sections.head: Firms, not lone rangers
sections.caption: who will cover the municipality beat
body: Ajay Shah had found the episode’s plan bleak and asked for some hope at the end. “I said we’ll do it in the last chapter. I lied,” Amit Varma said. {113-J05}
The conditions that created journalism and its values are gone, Varma said. The mainstream is crumbling everywhere, but nothing has taken its place.
Solo creators are filling some gaps. On Substack, he noted, “all your email IDs of your subscribers actually belong to you”. {#substack} Dhruv Rathee and Mohak Mangal do sense-making on YouTube.
## Who covers the municipality?

His worry is the vanishing beat. A local reporter who goes independent must learn video, marketing and thumbnails, and will soon be tempted by clicks. Individual passion, he said, produces only a few outliers. {113-C19}

Shah’s answer was firms: teams with a business model. The convincing successes so far, he said, are old media remade for the new age, such as the Financial Times, the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and The Economist.

~ He also relayed a hopeful theory from Suyash Rai. Radio was a weapon for Mussolini and Hitler before cultures absorbed it, and nobody now takes WhatsApp forwards seriously. Algorithms may follow, if people learn scepticism. {113-C20}

quote.text: But you can’t rely on individual passion and drive because that is a few outliers.

side.boxText: To prepare, Amit Varma spoke again to three former guests of *The Seen and the Unseen*: Prem Panicker, founding managing editor of Rediff and “a legend”, and the younger journalists Shephali Bhatt and Samarth Bansal. Credit them for anything good, he said. {#three}

contQuote.text: If you give the reader content, she will scroll. If you keep her attention, if you make her interesting, if you give her quality, she will scroll as much as you want her to scroll.

stories.caption: growing up among journalists
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s childhood in a journalists’ housing complex
stories.head: Eighty households, one calling
body: From the age of six until he left home at 17, Ajay Shah lived in a housing complex where 80 households all worked in the Indian media. {#eighty}

It was before television, so they were all in print, including Hindi, Marathi and Gujarati papers. Amit Varma would not name the famous enclave, lest “admiring nubile young women” land up at Shah’s house. {113-J01}

Shah’s father worked at the Economic Times, which then had a serious research department, the Economic Times Research Bureau. K.A. Antony, formerly of the RBI, created it and brought Shah’s father in; when Antony died, Shah’s father became its second head.
Top economists edited the paper, among them Hanan Ezekiel, “brother of the much more famous Nissim Ezekiel”. {113-J17}

The Times of India grew up around Shamlal and Girilal Jain, whose dense opinion pieces the whole country read. Shah compared their influence to that of France’s philosophers in the 1960s. These, he said, were the people who shaped the collective consciousness.

He was ten when the Emergency came. The Indian Express carried empty white space rather than print what the censors wanted. {#blank} Later, a full-page investigation on the Express’s front page by Arun Shourie, into A.R. Antulay’s trusts, cost the Maharashtra chief minister his job.

~ Journalists were poorly paid, and there was little profit in the trade. But it was, Shah said, “fully a noble calling”. “It was about being good, valuable participants in the emergence of a good society.”
stories.why: Journalism as a noble calling is not a myth: within living memory, editors shaped how a nation thought. Varma added a caveat. Such nostalgia is selective, he said, and not everything was rosy then. {#rosy}

stories.start: Like when I grew up in the eighties and nineties, my impression of journalism
stories.end: There is no striving for a different frontier.
stories.caption: the question in the press box
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the golden age that wasn’t
stories.head: Two words or three?
body: Growing up in the 1980s and 1990s, Amit Varma thought of journalism as the place for people who could not get into engineering, medicine or the UPSC. Many old-school journalists he later worked with could not write a proper English sentence.

At the Chinnaswami Stadium in Bangalore, a noted journalist from the Hindu, “very nice guy”, once sidled up to him during a cricket match. He asked: “Amit, tell me something, is nevertheless two words or three words?” {113-J03}
Varma admits he was arrogant with some of them, and regrets it. The legends were real: Arun Shourie, Vir Sanghvi at Sunday, India Today’s copy desk under Dilip Bobb. {113-S07}
~ But before the internet, readers had no New Yorker or Economist to compare with. Low standards fed low expectations, which fed lower standards.

quote.text: But these are outliers. This is a selection bias playing out in our memory. We remember the good names.

stories.start: I remember two prominent examples of this, and many journalists that we know
stories.end: But that is the very reason it was sort of spiked.
stories.caption: sacked editors and police at the door
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what happens when the powerful are annoyed
stories.head: A knock for every byline
body: Amit Varma gave two examples of the state’s stick, both from the HT group. When Mint launched, its editor Raju Narisetti wrote something that angered P. Chidambaram, who had him sacked. Narisetti left the country. {113-S11}
Years later, under the BJP, Bobby Ghosh ran a tracker of hate crimes at the Hindustan Times. Arun Jaitley allegedly disliked it, and Ghosh was sacked too.

Then Shephali Bhatt told Varma about a Financial Times exposé of a leading business family. Within a day, police visited every Indian name on the byline. The foreign lead correspondent went back to her previous posting.
~ And a friend’s investigative story, which everyone called explosive, was spiked at the last minute. “But that is the very reason it was sort of spiked,” Varma said. {113-J04}
stories.why: The state’s stick is real, used by both parties, and works mostly through quiet pressure. It explains, Varma said, why small independent outlets with nothing to lose are often the ones showing a spine. {113-J16}
stories.postscript: Varma was unsure whether “if you ain’t got nothing, you got nothing to lose” came from Dylan, Joan Baez or Kris Kristofferson.

stories.start: I tried this once where I decided I'll go into cookie right wing thinking
stories.end: narrows down to one tiny sliver, and even that may not be true.
stories.caption: his two YouTube feeds
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s experiment with the algorithm
stories.head: Separate feeds, separate worlds
body: Amit Varma wanted to see what the kooky right-wing ecosystem on YouTube looked like. So he opened an incognito window and logged in with another Gmail account. {113-S14}
He now has two YouTube feeds. “There has never been a common thing that has come up,” he said. They are different worlds.

That is his worry about algorithms, which feed you more of whatever you click. A 15-year-old boy who clicks on one misogynistic, rabble-rousing piece can end up in a bubble of such content, and take it for reality. {113-C18}

~ When Varma wrote against demonetisation in the Times of India, someone else wrote a column for it, “which is as it should be”. In separate feeds, each side will think the other evil, and from inside its own world, that is reasonable.

quote.text: your knowledge of the world narrows down to one tiny sliver, and even that may not be true.

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah’s antidote is three printed newspapers each morning, read with coffee “like a civilised person”.

quiz.q: What did the editor of a major Indian newspaper say his paper’s job was?
quiz.a: To comfort the comforted, the reverse of journalism’s motto. He meant it seriously.

quiz.q: At Yahoo India, what drew 450 to 500 million page views a month on its own?
quiz.a: OMG, a section of Bollywood party photographs from one Bombay photographer.

quiz.q: Why did Amit Varma refuse to split articles across several pages at Cricinfo?
quiz.a: Readers scroll for quality content; making them click again is, he said, rude.

quiz.q: What is Gell-Mann amnesia, the effect Amit Varma described in the trust chapter?
quiz.a: Spotting errors on your own subject, then trusting the rest of the paper anyway.

quiz.q: Which Indian media company did Ajay Shah call the cleanest test of the clickbait model?
quiz.a: Bennett Coleman: it had the scale, went all in, and its profit declined.

quiz.q: Which album did Ajay Shah recommend, and what book inspired it, by his account?
quiz.a: Roger Waters’s *Amused to Death*, written after Waters read Neil Postman’s book.
